Addition Facts.context_blurb:
Addition facts are the small sums you want to know instantly, without counting on your fingers. Three tricks cover most of them. Adding 0 changes nothing. Adding 10 only bumps the tens digit up by one. For everything else, make a ten first: split the smaller number so that part of it tops the bigger number up to a round ten, then add what is left over. Doubles (a number plus itself) are worth memorizing, because a near-double is just one more or one less than a double you already know.

Worked example with bigger numbers: 28 + 7. Give 2 of the 7 to the 28 to make 30. That leaves 5 still to add, so the answer is 35.

Subtraction Facts.context_blurb:
Subtraction asks how far apart two numbers are. For small facts, think of addition running backwards: to take a number away, ask what you would add to it to get back to where you started. Taking away 0 leaves a number alone, and any number minus itself is 0. When the two numbers are close together, it is quicker to count up from the smaller one than to count down from the bigger one.

Worked example with bigger numbers: 43 - 38. Count up from 38. Adding 2 reaches 40, and 3 more reaches 43. You added 5 altogether, so the gap is 5.

Missing Numbers.context_blurb:
A missing-number question hides one piece of a sum and asks you to find it. The key idea is the fact family: three numbers that belong together give four facts. If 30 + 12 = 42, then 12 + 30 = 42, and also 42 - 30 = 12 and 42 - 12 = 30. So when a piece of an addition is missing, subtract the piece you know from the total. When the missing piece is the number being taken away, subtract the answer from the starting number.

Worked example: 42 - ? = 30. The missing piece is whatever separates 42 from 30, which is 42 - 30. The answer is 12.

Skip Counting.context_blurb:
Skip counting means jumping forward by the same amount every time: by 2s, by 5s, by 10s and so on. To find the next number, take the last one and add the step. It is the bridge between adding and multiplying, because the fourth jump of a step is the same as four lots of it.

Patterns help you check yourself. Counting by 10s always ends in 0. Counting by 5s always ends in 5 or 0. Counting by 2s (from zero) always stays even.

Worked example: counting by 9s from zero goes 9, 18, 27, 36. Each step adds 9, which is the same as adding 10 and stepping back 1.

Times Tables.context_blurb:
A times-table fact counts equal groups, and the order never matters: seven groups of three is the same total as three groups of seven. A few shortcuts carry most of the table. Anything times 0 is 0. Times 1 leaves a number alone. Times 2 is a double, and times 4 is a double of a double. Times 5 is half of times 10. Times 9 is times 10 with one group taken off.

When a fact slips your mind, build it from facts you do know.

Worked example with a bigger number: 14 × 3. Ten threes are 30 and four threes are 12. Add them: 42.

Division Facts.context_blurb:
Division undoes multiplication. Asking how many 7s fit into a number is the same as asking what you multiply 7 by to make it. That means every times-table fact you know hands you two division facts for free. Dividing by 1 leaves a number alone, and any number divided by itself is 1.

If the answer does not come straight away, build up to it in chunks you know.

Worked example with a bigger number: 91 ÷ 7. Ten 7s make 70. That leaves 21, which is three more 7s. Ten and three make 13, so the answer is 13.

Adding and Subtracting Tens.context_blurb:
Adding or taking away a multiple of 10 only changes the tens digit. The ones digit never moves. Think of the tens as a stack of blocks: 30 is three tens, so adding 30 puts three more blocks on the stack, and subtracting 30 takes three off.

If the stack goes past nine tens, the extra rolls over into the hundreds, exactly like ones rolling over into tens.

Worked example with bigger numbers: 147 + 30. The 4 tens become 7 tens and the 7 ones stay put, giving 177. Going the other way, 177 - 50 takes five tens off the stack and leaves 127.

Doubling and Halving.context_blurb:
To double a number, double each place value separately and add the results. To halve a number, split it into hundreds, tens and ones, halve each piece and add them back together. If a piece is odd, remember that half of one ten is 5 and half of one hundred is 50.

These two moves are worth practising because so much else is built from them: multiplying by 4 is doubling twice, and dividing by 4 is halving twice.

Worked example with bigger numbers: twice 136 is 200 plus 60 plus 12, which is 272. Half of 174 is 50 plus 35 plus 2, which is 87.

Rounding.context_blurb:
Rounding swaps a number for the nearest tidy one. First decide which place you are rounding to, then look at the digit just to its right. If that digit is 0 to 4, round down: the place stays as it is and everything after it becomes zeros. If that digit is 5 to 9, round up: the place goes up by one and everything after it becomes zeros. If the place was a 9, it rolls over and carries into the next place, just as in addition.

So for the nearest 10 you look at the ones digit, and for the nearest 100 you look at the tens digit.

Worked example: 2,847. To the nearest 10, the ones digit is 7, so round up to 2,850. To the nearest 100, the tens digit is 4, so round down to 2,800.

Two-Digit Addition and Subtraction.context_blurb:
Work one place value at a time. To add, add the tens, add the ones, then combine. If the ones come to more than 9, carry the extra ten across. To subtract when the top ones digit is too small, borrow: unwrap one ten into ten ones and carry on.

A faster route in your head is round-and-fix. Add or subtract a friendly round number instead, then correct for the difference.

Worked examples with bigger numbers: 368 + 247. The hundreds make 500, the tens make 100, the ones make 15, for 615 in total. And 532 - 198: take away 200 to get 332, then give back the 2 you over-subtracted, for 334.

Multiplying by Parts.context_blurb:
Big multiplications come apart into small ones. Split the larger number into hundreds, tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add the results. This is called the distributive rule, and it is how people multiply in their heads.

When both numbers have two digits, split just one of them and treat the other as a single block.

Worked example with a bigger number: 136 × 7. One hundred 7s are 700, thirty 7s are 210, and six 7s are 42. Add them: 952.

A neat variation is to round one number and fix it afterwards: 99 lots of something is 100 lots with one lot taken away.

Order of Operations.context_blurb:
When a sum mixes operations, the order is fixed, and it is not simply left to right. Brackets come first. Then powers. Then multiplication and division, working left to right. Last of all, addition and subtraction, working left to right.

The rule exists so that everyone reading the same line of maths gets the same answer.

Worked example: 20 - 3 × 5 + 4. Do the multiplication first: 3 × 5 is 15. The line is now 20 - 15 + 4. Then go left to right: 20 - 15 is 5, and 5 + 4 is 9. Reading the original straight across would give 89, which is wrong.

Negative Numbers.context_blurb:
Picture a number line with zero in the middle. Adding moves you right, subtracting moves you left, and the negative numbers sit to the left of zero. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: taking away a debt leaves you better off. That is the only time two minus signs make a plus. A sum like -30 - 40 is just two moves to the left, landing on -70.

For multiplying and dividing, work out the size as usual and then fix the sign. If the two signs match, the answer is positive. If they differ, the answer is negative.

Worked examples: for -34 + 19, start at -34 and move 19 to the right, landing on -15. For -12 × -11, the signs match, so the answer is positive: 132.

Simplifying Fractions.context_blurb:
A ratio or fraction is in its simplest form when no number bigger than 1 divides both parts. To get there, find the largest number that goes into both parts (the greatest common divisor) and divide both by it. If you cannot spot the largest one straight away, divide by any common factor and keep going until nothing more works.

Dividing both parts by the same number never changes the ratio. It only makes it easier to read and compare.

Worked example: 84:126. Both are even, so halve them to get 42:63. Both of those divide by 3, giving 14:21, and then by 7, which leaves 2:3.

Fractions, Decimals and Percents.context_blurb:
A fraction, a decimal and a percent are three ways of writing the same amount, and you can move between them. Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom. Some divisions never finish and the digits repeat; round those to three decimal places. Decimal to percent: move the decimal point two places to the right. Percent to decimal: move it two places to the left.

Some conversions come up so often that they are worth knowing by heart: halves, quarters, fifths, tenths and eighths.

Worked example: 7/20. Dividing 7 by 20 gives 0.35. Moving the point two places right gives 35%. Going back the other way, 35% means 35 out of 100, which simplifies to 7/20 again.

Fraction of a Quantity.context_blurb:
In maths, the word "of" means multiply. To take a fraction of a number, divide by the bottom number, which finds the size of one share, then multiply by the top number, which takes as many shares as you need.

When two fractions are chained together, you can either multiply the fractions first or simply take them one at a time, working from the right.

Worked examples: 5/9 of 108. One ninth of 108 is 12, and five of those make 60. For 2/3 of 3/4 of 96: three quarters of 96 is 72, and two thirds of 72 is 48.

Fraction Arithmetic.context_blurb:
To add or subtract fractions, they must have the same bottom number. Rewrite each fraction over a common denominator, then add or subtract only the tops. To multiply fractions, multiply the tops together and the bottoms together. To divide, flip the second fraction upside down and multiply instead. Simplify the answer at the end.

Worked examples: 5/6 + 3/8. Both bottoms go into 24, so rewrite as 20/24 + 9/24, which is 29/24. For 5/6 ÷ 3/8, flip the second fraction and multiply: 5/6 × 8/3 is 40/18, which simplifies to 20/9.

Percent of a Number.context_blurb:
Percent means "out of 100". The anchor is 10%: move the decimal point one place to the left. Almost everything else is built from that. 5% is half of 10%. 20% is double it. 25% is a quarter of the number, 50% is half of it, and 75% is a half plus a quarter.

For an awkward percent, split it into pieces you can do and add them up.

Worked example: 35% of 2,600. 10% is 260, so 30% is 780. 5% is half of 260, which is 130. Together that is 910.

One more trick: percents can be swapped around. 4% of 75 is exactly the same as 75% of 4.

Finding the Percent.context_blurb:
Two related questions live here. The first is "what percent of the whole is this part?" Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. The second is "by what percent did it change?" Find the size of the change, divide by the starting value (never the new one), then multiply by 100.

Worked examples: what percent of 320 is 48? Dividing 48 by 320 gives 0.15, so it is 15%. Now a price rises from 320 to 368. The change is 48, and 48 divided by the starting 320 is 0.15, a 15% increase. Dropping from 368 back to 320 is a smaller percent, because the starting value is larger.

Squares, Cubes and Powers.context_blurb:
A power is repeated multiplication. Squaring a number multiplies it by itself. Cubing uses it three times. The small raised number (or the number after the ^ sign) tells you how many copies to multiply together.

Powers of 10 are a 1 followed by that many zeros. Powers of 2 keep doubling, so each one is twice the one before. Squares up to 20 and cubes up to 10 are worth memorizing.

You can also rebuild a square from its neighbour: the next square is the last one plus the two numbers added together.

Worked example: thirty-one squared. Thirty squared is 900. Add 30 and 31 to get 961.

Square and Cube Roots.context_blurb:
A root undoes a power. The square root of a number is the value that, multiplied by itself, gives that number. The cube root is the value that gives it when used three times. So roots are the squares and cubes you already know, read backwards.

If you are unsure, trap the answer between two squares you do know, then use the last digit to narrow it down.

Worked example: the square root of 1,764. Forty squared is 1,600 and forty-five squared is 2,025, so the root lies between 40 and 45. The number ends in 4, so the root must end in 2 or 8. Try 42: it works.

Exponent Rules.context_blurb:
When you multiply powers of the same base, add the exponents. You are simply counting how many copies of the base there are altogether. When you divide, subtract the exponents, because copies on the top and bottom cancel each other out. The base itself never changes.

Worked examples: 7^3 × 7^2. Three 7s multiplied by two more 7s is five 7s, so the answer is 7^5, which works out to 16,807. For 7^6 ÷ 7^4, four of the six copies cancel, leaving 7^2, which is 49.

The rule only works when the bases match. A power of 2 times a power of 5 cannot be combined this way; you have to work each one out.

Divisibility Rules.context_blurb:
These are quick tests for whether a number divides evenly, with no long division.

2: the last digit is even.
3: the digits add up to a multiple of 3.
4: the last two digits form a multiple of 4.
5: the number ends in 0 or 5.
6: it passes both the 2 test and the 3 test.
8: the last three digits form a multiple of 8.
9: the digits add up to a multiple of 9.
11: subtract and add the digits in turn; the result is 0 or a multiple of 11.
12: it passes both the 3 test and the 4 test.

For 7 there is no easy test, so just divide.

Worked example: 5,238. It is even, and 5 + 2 + 3 + 8 = 18, a multiple of 9. So 2, 3, 6 and 9 all divide it.

One-Step Equations.context_blurb:
An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. To get x on its own, undo what was done to it using the opposite operation. If something was added, subtract it. If something was subtracted, add it. If x was multiplied, divide. If x was divided, multiply.

Always check by putting your answer back into the original equation.

Worked examples: x + 47 = 112. Subtract 47 from both sides to get x = 65. For x/9 = 14, multiply both sides by 9 to get x = 126. Check: 126 divided by 9 is 14.

Two-Step Equations.context_blurb:
Undo the operations in the reverse of the order they were done, like taking off your shoes before your socks. When x has been multiplied and then had something added, undo the adding first and the multiplying second.

When there are brackets with a number outside, you have a choice: divide both sides by the outside number first, or multiply the bracket out. Dividing first is usually quicker.

Worked examples: 9x + 14 = 131. Subtract 14 to get 9x = 117, then divide by 9 to get x = 13. For 9(x - 6) = 72, divide by 9 to get x - 6 = 8, then add 6 to get x = 14.

Pythagorean Triples.context_blurb:
In a right-angled triangle, the two shorter sides (the legs) and the longest side (the hypotenuse) always obey one rule: square each leg, add the squares, and you get the square of the hypotenuse. A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that fits this rule exactly.

A handful of triples turn up again and again, and any multiple of a triple is also a triple: double or triple every side and the rule still holds. So when you are given two sides, look for a familiar triple that has been scaled up.

Worked example: legs of 20 and 21. The squares are 400 and 441, which add to 841. That is 29 squared, so the hypotenuse is 29.

Sum of 1 to N.context_blurb:
To add every whole number from 1 up to some number n, pair them off: the first with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. Every pair adds up to the same total, n + 1, and there are n/2 pairs. That gives the formula n(n + 1)/2. When n is odd, one number in the middle is left without a partner, but the formula still gives the right answer: multiply n by n + 1, then halve.

The story goes that the mathematician Gauss spotted this as a schoolboy, when his teacher set the class to add up the numbers from 1 to 100 to keep them busy.

Worked example: adding 1 through 60. Each pair totals 61 and there are 30 pairs, so the sum is 30 × 61, which is 1,830.
